The original record for 2023-04-19 pointed to only one file: `git/object_scanner.go`. The file header showed `package git` and `import (`. The search terms were written as a list: scanner, line, object, oid, err, eof. > First check what a line read by the scanner looks like. The object and path should be retained at this layer; err needs to stay with the record. Check again at eof; do not assume from memory that there are no objects left. The actual include / exclude calls have not been found yet.

This passage preserved only the direction for verification. It did not specify the complete record format or who assembles the revision set. Inspect the file's own declarations first, note its immediate neighbors first, and document call relationships only after finding references.

## Three questions were initially crammed together

The earliest page put "how a line is split, how the object identifier is retained, and how the include and exclude revision sets change the scan scope" in the same place. Looking back now, these three questions are not at the same layer: the first two concern the scanner's record boundaries, while the last also involves the caller's selection of revision sets. At the time, there was not enough material to bring them into a single decision, but the page already showed traces of this conflation.

During that investigation, a narrowly scoped sequence was written in the margin: starting from `internal/history-core`'s `v_prev`, open `git/object_scanner.go`, record the file header and immediate neighbors, then find an actual call to confirm whether the usual entry point passes through here. This sequence was not treated as a general process for the project, but merely as a working record to avoid jumping directly from an issue name to a conclusion.

The file location can lead someone back to the local code; it cannot, on its own, establish who calls it, nor can it establish that the input revision set has already been filtered. This limitation existed from the first scrap of paper, but it was not spelled out separately at the time.

## Two earlier judgments in the first draft

The early text described "reading to the end" as though it were an ordinary record. The original sentence was:

> When there is no new line, it may be the last object; start by examining the return value with this possibility in mind.

The same section also said:

> include and exclude may be merged inside the scanner; just keep looking in the same place.

[Deprecated] These two sentences must not be used as the current interface description. The first did not distinguish an end signal from emitting a record, and the second lumped set selection together with record parsing. They were not deleted because the subsequent review began with precisely these two misreadings; deleting the original sentences would instead obscure why the issues were mixed together at the time.

Another older example is shorter still, saying only "pass include / exclude to the scanner together first". No call path, parameter values or results follow. It can only indicate the working assumption at the time, and cannot indicate that a confirmed compatible invocation method exists.

## File Review Addendum

The set reopened on 2023-10-02 was still `internal/history-core`,`v_prev`,`git/object_scanner.go`. The old note beside the references was also left unchanged: the old investigation records point here based on issue names and call names, and the actual relationship is still determined by the references in that revision.

The review started at the top of the file. What could be directly confirmed was `package git` and `import (`. Searches were then run using scanner, line, object, oid, err, eof, extra, object. as terms. This yielded local declarations and clues from adjacent code, not a complete call graph. Directory locations, search hits or field names were not treated as proof of a caller.

This version still uses more tentative wording. "The termination branch should be checked" means the review is not yet complete; it did not prematurely add "there will be no extra objects" to the assessment made in 2023. The review side note from 2023-10-03 did not request that the old paragraphs be deleted. It focused on the habit of "pointing to files based on issue names and call names": this can be retained as a historical search clue, but does not establish an implementation relationship. Continuing to treat include, exclude as the scanner's own responsibility would make the page shorter, but would incorrectly attribute choices made at the calling layer to the parsing layer; recording only the scanner's local behavior and leaving set selection to a review of the actual calls would leave gaps in the page, but every decision could be traced back to a visible entry point. > If include and exclude appear at the same time, first check whether scanner's result has already been filtered; the caller's parameters do not need to be split apart for now.

[Later overturned] This passage treated "the input has already been filtered" as a premise, but did not say who performed the filtering. The early draft conflated it with "no new lines" in a single sentence, but that wording was later dropped. As of 2025-08-28, the page can no longer use "it should be able to retain object identifiers and paths" as its definitive statement. That sentence remains in the earlier historical layer, while the current requirement is placed after the historical material to prevent readers from conflating the initial draft's assumptions with behavior verified later.

The current record boundary is stated as:

> RevListScanner parses each rev-list line into a 40-hex object ID and path, exposes OID/Name/Err, and reaches EOF without emitting an extra object.

This sentence appears explicitly only once in this version. It resolves two open questions from the early draft: each rev-list line yields a 40-hex object ID and path; OID, Name, and Err are the fields retained; no extra object is emitted out of nowhere when EOF is reached. It does not attribute collection selection by include and exclude to the scanner, nor does it change the temporal context of the preceding older paragraphs.

The precise sentence is placed here, rather than backfilled into the scraps of paper from 2023. The early version did indeed complete only a less rigorous review; only the current version is justified in using this explicit record boundary. The "should" in the old paragraph coexists with the precise wording in the current version, showing exactly how our understanding converged.

## Local relationships settled now

The decisions in this version are split between two adjacent but distinct entry points.

The first is record parsing. For each line entering the scanner, what is checked is the correspondence among object ID, path, OID, Name, and Err. Normal records are checked by their field values, abnormal records by Err, and termination by whether the EOF branch still has no extra objects. This is the interface boundary that can now be recorded directly on this page.

The second is revision sets. The include and exclude revision sets remain a selection issue at the calling layer. We need to find actual calls and record how the sets are passed in and what results users see; without this material, we cannot say that the sets are merged inside the scanner, nor can we conversely say that they are necessarily prefiltered by the caller.

The two lines intersect at the input records, not at a responsibility that can be arbitrarily reassigned. Calling Fang Ke can change the range of revisions sent to the scanner, but the material already on this page is only sufficient to explain how the scanner observes the lines it receives. It is not sufficient to establish the order in which include and exclude are combined, nor the specific effect of partial-history parent retention on the input set.

This distinction also explains why the title is still a history of requirements, rather than a final conclusion. The title retains the subject from when the page was created, while the body preserves the process by which our understanding changed from "looking for all the issues in the same place" to "separating the record boundary from the selection entry point". The precise boundary that can actually be cited directly appears only in the current-version passage further down.

## Diagram preserved from the actual work

The diagram below is not a call graph. It only places the already-separated record path and the still-incomplete set selection side by side; the arrow from `RevisionSetChoice` to `UnconfirmedBoundary` deliberately does not point to the scanner's fields, because this page has no call results that could establish exactly how data is passed between the two.

stateDiagram-v2

    RevListLine --> RecordFields: local parse
    RevListLine --> ErrorExit: Err path

## A few remarks on the sidelines of the meeting

The margin of the page also contains a passage that was not compiled into formal meeting minutes:

> Do not work backward from the term `include` to infer the filtering location yet. First get a clear picture of the scanner records; obtain the caller results separately. If we look only at `git/object_scanner.go`, at most we can make firm statements about the local fields and the EOF boundary.

This marginal note is consistent with the decision made after the review, but it is not a new behavioral provision. The meeting did not leave behind a complete test table that could be reconstructed from this, so the note is retained only to explain why the conclusions were not extended further at the time.

Another remark is even shorter: "A path is an entry point, not the answer." It was not elevated to an interface specification, and only explains why the old paragraph is still retained. File locations can help trace back to record parsing, but cannot replace the call graph; field names can help trace back to the error and termination branches, but cannot replace user-facing results.

## Adjacent questions left in place

1. As for whether actual day-to-day calls pass through this scanner, this page currently provides only local path clues and lacks citable call results.
2. When include and exclude appear together, how the revision order selection and set boundaries are passed along needs to be checked against the adjacent interface records for DOC-12, and cannot be assessed from the scanner file alone.
3. As for whether partial-history parent retention changes the set of incoming rev-list lines, this page has no material on which to base a judgment, and does not describe it as parser behavior.

5. The direct dependencies in the file header provide only clues at the level of `package git` and `import (`, and an unrecorded call tree cannot be reconstructed from two lines of declarations.

An old troubleshooting note proposed "fetching once more after reading to the end". It was not supported by a code snippet, nor did it explain whether an object would be produced. The EOF boundary was later reviewed separately, making this approach obsolete, but it is retained in the appendix as a historical example.

# Revision Ordering and Parent-Chain Proposal

This interface review first separates two questions that are easy to conflate: who chooses the order for traversing revisions, and whether the parent-commit boundary should remain in the result when only part of the history is available.

There are two candidates for ordering. One is to have callers pass the command-side ordering argument directly; the other is for the interface to accept only a limited ordering value and have the traversal layer translate it into a command option. The former avoids one conversion layer, but callers will start depending on command text. The latter is narrower and makes it easier to refuse to change the existing traversal when an unknown value appears.

The parent-chain question cannot be decided along with the ordering option. A partial-history result may need to tell the upstream layer "there is still a parent boundary here," or it may need to include only the currently visible commits; that depends on whether the caller uses the result for display, filtering, or continued tracing. The initial draft leans toward retaining the boundary information to avoid premature truncation at the interface layer, but there are not yet enough samples to show that every entry point needs it.

The initial plan is to draft a mapping for limited ordering values and leave unrecognized inputs with no ordering option. Parent-chain retention will be tracked separately as an experiment: first confirm whether result consumers actually read parent commits, then decide the return structure. If the mapping requires the caller to pass an additional command fragment, or the parent-chain proposal forces existing consumers to distinguish between two result sets, revert to the original interface first.

The initial draft treated "ordering" as an ordinary switch inside the traverser; that assessment needs to be retracted. After reviewing the parameter entry points near the interface, the ordering value looks more like command semantics explicitly chosen by the caller. - The interface accepts a limited set of ordering values, and the traversal layer maintains the mapping. The mapping location is clear; unknown values can leave the option unset.

# Revision Ordering and Parent-Chain Proposal

Order selection and parent chains for partial history came up in the same review, but the changes should not share a fallback branch. The former is about converting interface values into command arguments; the latter is about how much structure the result set should retain at gaps in the history. Leaving both for the traversal layer to "handle along the way" would make callers unable to tell whether they were getting a change in ordering or a change in boundaries.

The previous version retained an imprecise claim: as long as the order value could be passed down to the lower layer, its meaning could be decided later. That approach was not carried forward. The code near the parameter entry point uses `vendor/github.com/spf13/pflag/flag.go`, whose package name is `pflag`, and integrates it into the parameter definitions through `flag "github.com/ogier/pflag"`. This is not the place to set rules for History Ledger, but the follow-up review showed that order selection should happen once in the interface adapter, rather than leaving each call site to assemble its own command arguments.

## Trial Scope for Order Values

The trial only accepts order values already named by the interface. If the adapter finds a matching entry, it adds the corresponding command argument; if the interface supplies no value, no argument is added; if an unsupported value is supplied, no argument is added either. Leaving the order unset does not request a new default, and unknown values should not silently fall back to an ordering that seems reasonable.

The current requirement is stated as follows so implementation and review use the same semantics:

RevListOrder values map to their documented command flags, while an unset or unsupported order leaves the flag disabled.

This requirement rules out two shortcuts discussed earlier. The first is to treat the interface value directly as command text: it saves writing a mapping, but allows unsupported values to bypass the interface boundary. The second is to supply a fixed order for empty values: it appears to make results stable, but actually changes existing entry points that have expressed no ordering preference. Neither approach is included in this trial.

The adapter needs to retain a very small mapping surface, rather than pushing command-line wrapper logic into consumers. This lets callers continue to express only their ordering intent, while the traversal implementation receives only confirmed arguments. If new order values appear later, define their command semantics first, then add them to the mapping. Do not reuse existing entries on the grounds that "a similar value already exists."

## Parent Commits Are Not a Side Effect of Ordering

Retaining parent commits in partial history remains a separate issue. The existing discussion establishes only this: at a parent boundary, consumers may interpret the result as indicating that the history is still incomplete, rather than simply treating parent entries as part of a normal commit set. The initial draft favored retention, but the follow-up review did not turn that preference into a general rule.

At least two types of consumers need to be distinguished here. Entry points that read only the current commit set may not need any extra parent entries; entry points that continue tracing gaps in history may depend on the parent boundary to continue navigating. The available material does not establish that these two types of entry points can share the same return shape, so neither "retain all" nor "trim all" will be specified in the ordering interface.

This round allows a trial of a candidate implementation that retains parent-chain information, with checks of the fields consumers actually read. The focus is not the number of parent entries, but whether boundary information is used as a hint for continued tracing. If a consumer only needs the current set, it should not be forced to handle additional parent structure to accommodate another entry point.

The hands-on investigation into commit-only traversal is documented separately in DOC-13; its branches are not treated here as evidence for the parent-chain policy. Both issues involve revision traversal, but one concerns the scope of the objects traversed, while the other concerns how boundaries are represented in partial-history results.

## Stop Conditions

If any of the following occurs in the order mapping, do not expand the trial further: callers need to supply additional arguments not named by the interface; the implementation silently converts an unset value into an ordering; or an unsupported value still changes the command arguments. In that case, return to the original behavior with no added arguments, then complete the definitions of the interface values.

For the parent-chain trial, use what consumers read as the criterion. If retaining parent information requires extra branching in entry points that originally used only the commit set, split the parent-chain adjustment out of this round first; if no entry point can be confirmed to read boundary information, do not expand the returned content based on guesswork either. The goal of this proposal is only to give order selection a clear entry point, without creating a hard-to-reverse default answer to the parent-chain question in partial history.

# Commit Traversal and JSON Troubleshooting Tree

This review did not rewrite the old notes as conclusions, but only clarified where to stop for the two symptoms. The revision traversal anomaly still starts with "fewer records than expected", and the rename entry in status JSON still starts with "fields do not match". They can occur in the same incident, but one troubleshooting action should not replace the other.

## What to Obtain First, and What to Assess Next

When receiving a report of "only commit", first ask three questions about the immediate context: whether the request includes revision, whether the scanner actually received revision, and what arguments were passed to `rev-list`. Early records only documented the results, without preserving the correspondence among these three, so "too few objects" was once misread as objects being unreadable.

Now keep records in the following order:

1. Record `ScanRefsOptions` from the request as is, including only items that actually have values.
2. Keep the `rev-list` arguments separately, without mixing them into the result summary.
3. Clearly state whether the results contain revision records, commit records, or a record form that cannot be classified.
4. If the incident also includes status JSON, save the original JSON separately, not in the same sample as the arguments.

Here, "as is" only means not replacing field names or omitting parameters before troubleshooting. It does not require archiving requests from every caller. If part of a request is available, first compare that part with the arguments from the same scan; if either of these two objects is unavailable, stop at that gap.

## revision Branch

```text
Fewer scan records than expected
├─ The request has no revision
│  └─ Go back to the ref prefix or caller parameters; do not investigate beyond the scanner
├─ The request has revision, but the scanner did not receive it
│  └─ Save the request and observations at the entry point, and stop before entering the scanner
├─ The scanner received revision, but the records contain only commit
│  ├─ Obtain ScanRefsOptions
│  ├─ Obtain the rev-list arguments
│  └─ Compare the request's intent with the actual parameters
└─ The request and arguments match, but the results still cannot be explained
   └─ Keep the record excerpt and code location, without first attributing the issue to packed fallback
```

The initial draft treated "the results contain only commit" as a signal that `objects` might have been omitted. This signal can still be retained, but the order has changed: it can only be used after the request options and arguments have been examined. The form of the results alone cannot distinguish between an intentionally selected record type, parameters not reaching the entry point, or a problem in the object-reading path.

If revision never entered `lfs/gitscanner_refs.go` at all, further examination of the object database will not help. What needs to be retained at this point is the revision in the request, the parameters passed by the caller, and the observation that the scanner entry point did not receive it. If revision did enter, first look for differences between the request options and arguments; when differences exist, the subject of investigation is parameter construction, not packed fallback.

If the arguments look complete, still do not fill in the cause on this page as some kind of storage-layer failure. The current material only supports requiring that the records and entry-point location be retained. The code snippet obtained next time can be attached beside this record, but do not replace the snippet itself with the four-character phrase "parameters are normal".

### Old Order (Retained)

> If the results contain only commit, first treat the object database as unreadable.

This passage comes from the earliest on-call notes. At the time, it provided a direction for further action, but did not explain whether the request originally wanted only commit, nor did it compare `ScanRefsOptions` with the `rev-list` arguments. After the review, it is no longer placed at the first level of the tree, but it has not been deleted: when similar descriptions come up later, it still shows why the early approach went straight to the object-reading path.

During the same period, there was also a practice of "check packed fallback first". It did not explain parameter differences, so it is no longer the default first step. Only after the request intent, arguments, and record form have been examined, and clear indications still point to object reading, is it worth opening a separate object-storage investigation; this page does not have enough material to turn that direction into a fixed procedure.

## status JSON Branch

The rename entry needs its own original copy. After obtaining JSON, record the field names actually present in the entry, its position in JSON, the adjacent objects, and which entry point it came from. A field name looking like an old field does not mean the current entry point guarantees that field; a field name not looking like an old field does not mean this is a rename error.

```text
A rename entry appears in status JSON
├─ The original JSON is available
│  ├─ Mark the field names and entry position
│  ├─ Record the adjacent objects
│  └─ If it is an old entry point, record the entry-point differences separately
└─ Only a secondhand account or partial text from a screenshot is available
   └─ Record that a sample is missing, and stop interpreting field semantics
```

Finding the revision request first is not required here. The JSON sample itself is enough to start checking fields; conversely, no matter how complete the revision arguments are, they cannot supply the actual fields of the rename entry. If both kinds of material are available in the incident, give them separate record blocks to avoid later treating a particular parameter choice as evidence of changes to JSON fields.

The earliest approach tended to look for the rename entry directly using familiar old field names. This is no longer suitable as the default action, because the original JSON was not retained at the time. Old samples can still be placed alongside as historical references, but first record what actually appears in the new sample, then discuss whether it matches the old entry point.

## Review Side Notes

This review focused on the order of evidence: attach the arguments before discussing object reading; retain JSON before discussing field compatibility. It did not verify all callers, nor did it provide a unified field table for the rename entry.

`lfs/gitscanner_refs.go` remains the starting point for tracing local relationships in the scanner. The file path can be used to locate where the request and `rev-list` parameters are adjacent, but cannot by itself establish ownership of the full implementation. If a new incident has only an issue name and a call name, with no request, arguments, or original JSON, state which item is missing, rather than filling the gaps with the old assumptions about objects.

## Items to Capture in the Next Update

- An excerpt of `ScanRefsOptions` from the same request and the `rev-list` arguments;
- An unmodified status JSON, showing the actual fields and position of the rename entry;
- A local record of "revision has entered, arguments have no differences, results are still sparse".

These three items are not a single unified issue. The first is for comparing parameters, the second is for JSON fields, and only the third might lead the investigation to a later reading path.

# Commit Traversal and JSON Troubleshooting Tree

This page gradually grew out of two very short field notes. Early on, someone wrote about revision traversal returning fewer results and the rename entry for status JSON in the same paragraph; each later addition changed only one of those breakpoints. The old conclusions were not removed, so as you read, you should not assume that the entire text reflects the position at a single point in time. Start with the symptoms and preserve the originals along their respective branches; the later paragraphs contain the most recently added check requirements.

## The Two Earliest Recorded Symptoms

The initial description consisted of just two sentences: the records returned by one scan did not match the caller's expectations and seemed to contain only commit; another observation noted that the rename entry for status JSON needed to be checked. Both the issue name and the call name led the investigation to `lfs/gitscanner_refs.go`.

At the time, the page treated this path as a shared entry point. The file header showed `package lfs`, as well as `import (` at the start of the direct dependencies. This was enough to direct the on-call staff back to the local code adjacent to the scanner, but not enough to answer how the caller assembled the request, nor could responsibility for the full implementation be inferred from the path name. The initial version did not distinguish between "navigating to a file" and "confirming that the file is responsible for a particular behavior", which is also why multiple follow-up notes were added later.

The early write-up mixed `rev-list`, `rev`, `list`, `commit`, and `objects` into a single record. When the results contained only commit, the first suspicion was that objects had not been passed in. That was a working hypothesis to help the investigation proceed, not a verified rule: at the time, no side-by-side record had been kept of `ScanRefsOptions` in the request and the arguments ultimately passed to `rev-list`, nor was there an original copy of status JSON available to recheck.

> Old note: For results containing only commit, initially treat this as missing objects and wait for the caller to reply.

This sentence is retained, not because it can still be followed as written, but because it was precisely the later counterexample checks that overturned the troubleshooting order it prescribed. The "missing objects" in the old record only shows that someone made that guess at the time, and cannot automatically be taken to mean that the object database was unreadable, that packed fallback failed, or that this was a fixed behavior of any particular caller.

## Entry Tree for 2023-03

The initial tree was very narrow, intended only to avoid sending requests that had not entered the scanner down the object-reading branch:

```text
Seeing relatively few revision records
├─ The request contains no revision
│  └─ Review the reference prefixes and caller arguments
├─ revision did not reach the scanner
│  └─ Stop before the entry point, save the request excerpt
├─ scanner has received revision, but only commit remains in the results
│  └─ Check whether the arguments to rev-list include objects
└─ Cannot see all the arguments
   └─ Capture the missing arguments first, do not attribute the results to a storage-layer cause
```

This version has a useful stopping point: when revision has not reached the scanner, you should not continue using the object database or packed fallback to fill in the cause. Request assembly before the entry point and object reads after the entry point are two different lines of investigation. But the third branch of the tree is still too coarse, treating "whether the arguments contain objects" and "what the request originally intended to scan" as the same question.

At the time the handling of status JSON was even more limited. The rename entry was only marked as "entry point pending verification", with no field examples, and there was not enough material to determine whether this was a field rename, a missing entry, or a difference between the old entry point and the current one. The original page correctly did not describe the JSON issue as a scanner failure, but it also did not provide a JSON record format that could be rechecked.

## Notes in the margins of the on-call page

Later on-call notes did not add a complete workflow, but only listed a few objects to save with the case: the `ScanRefsOptions` that actually had values in the request, the assembled `rev-list` arguments, exactly which kinds of records appeared in the results, and the unmodified status JSON.

These objects are not intended to provide a comprehensive description of the call chain. They each address a different misreading:

- `ScanRefsOptions` shows what the request layer actually selected;
- `rev-list` arguments show what arguments the scanner will use next;
- The result records show the observed form, not the cause;
- The original JSON shows the actual fields and location of the rename entry in that invocation of the entry point.

Saving only a results summary would make "only commit" look like a confirmed failure; saving only a textual paraphrase of JSON would make old field names look like current field names. The notes called for first preserving these originals separately, then comparing adjacent objects. They did not require collecting all four items for every case. If an item is missing, stop only on that branch.

During this period, there was also a brief on-call reminder: do not rename the original JSON and then use it for comparison. The field name of the rename entry and the objects adjacent to it should be recorded along with the original. When the original JSON is unavailable, all the page can do is state "missing sample"; do not fill in familiar old fields, let alone use revision scan results in place of the contents of JSON.

## An approach that went wrong

After the old tree was put into actual use, a faster but unsuccessful troubleshooting approach emerged: upon seeing that the records contained only commit, it attributed the problem directly to packed fallback, then looked for missing objects in the object database. This approach did not explain the difference between the request options and arguments, but instead conflated record type selection with object reads.

The review did not produce reusable command output, nor did it provide object counts or success logs. The conclusions that could be retained were very limited: that direct attribution could not account for the existing observations, and packed fallback should no longer be the default first step. The new sequence starts by returning to the request and arguments; if the two cannot be obtained, do not replace the unknown with "objects are unreadable".

This record also explains why the page still retains the old object database branch. It was the direction people at the time pursued for further investigation, but it cannot serve as the answer for every later "only commit" incident. Deleting the old section would mislead later readers into thinking that this page knew from the start that the parameters should be compared, obscuring how the understanding evolved.

### Deprecated handling approach: check the object database first

> If the results contain only commit, start by treating the object database as unreadable.

This old guidance is no longer suitable as the default action. It treats the form of the results as the cause of failure, yet does not first confirm whether the request intentionally limits the record types, nor does it confirm whether the `rev-list` arguments match the request options.

The old section can still serve as a follow-up direction under very narrow conditions: only when the request's intent is clear, the arguments do not differ from the request, and local records still point to object reads should a separate storage-layer check be initiated. There is not enough material here to specify how that check should be carried out, so do not rewrite it as a fixed object database operating procedure.

## Review sequence for 2023-08

The second pass separated "what the request asks for" from "what the scanner actually receives". The revision branch first asks whether revision enters `lfs/gitscanner_refs.go`, then retrieves `ScanRefsOptions`, and finally examines the `rev-list` arguments. Results containing only commit no longer lead straight to the conclusion that objects are missing.

```text
Fewer revision records than expected
├─ Request has no revision
│  └─ Go back to the reference prefix or caller arguments; stop before scanner
├─ Request has revision, but scanner did not receive it
│  └─ Preserve the request and entry-point observations; stop at the input path
├─ scanner received revision
│  ├─ Record the items in ScanRefsOptions that actually have values
│  ├─ Record the rev-list arguments
│  ├─ The two differ
│  │  └─ Stop at parameter assembly
│  └─ The two appear consistent
│     └─ Preserve the record shape; do not initially attribute it to packed fallback
└─ Request or arguments are missing
   └─ Record only the gap; do not infer object-read status
```

Here, "appears consistent" is not a success marker. It only means that this local evidence does not show an obvious difference between the option and the argument. If the result still cannot be explained, just retain the record fragment and code location. Without a new code fragment or caller result, "arguments are normal" should not be written as the final conclusion.

The review also listed status JSON separately. Investigating the rename entry does not start by looking for a familiar field; it starts by preserving the raw JSON and recording the actual field name, location, and adjacent objects where the entry appears. If the sample comes from an old entry point, record the entry-point difference separately; if there is only a textual description or an excerpted fragment, stop at the missing sample and do not fill in the field semantics.

```text
status JSON shows a rename entry
├─ Original JSON is available
│  ├─ Mark the entry's actual field name
│  ├─ Mark the entry's location and adjacent objects
│  └─ Record the old entry-point sample and current entry-point sample separately
└─ No original JSON
   └─ Log that the sample is missing; do not draw a conclusion from the old field
```

These two trees share only the action of "preserving the original first." The original material in the revision tree is the request, arguments, and records; the original material in the JSON tree is status JSON. Do not use a normal scan to prove that the rename entry is normal, and do not infer from a field anomaly that scanner missed the object.

## Rewording from the review

The review did not require creating a rule table covering all callers. The remaining requirements were very specific: include arguments first, then discuss object reads; retain JSON first, then discuss field compatibility. This order changes the location of the evidence; it does not put scanner, the object database, and the JSON entry under a single root cause.

After the review, the page divided observations into several distinct states:

- A request or `ScanRefsOptions` has been seen: this only shows that these actual values exist at the request layer;
- The `rev-list` arguments have been seen: this only shows that these contents appeared at the parameter layer;
- A returned record has been seen: this only shows the form of the result in the observed case;
- The raw JSON has been seen: only then can the actual fields and location of the rename entry be described;
- Only an issue name, call name, or secondhand account: the original material needed to support a conclusion about fields or parameters is still missing.

This format is not intended to add more layers to every investigation, but to prevent old issues from being mixed together again. For example, the absence of an item from arguments cannot be judged erroneous independently of the request type; an old field in JSON also cannot be treated as a current commitment without the entry version.

One review side note is especially important to retain: `lfs/gitscanner_refs.go` is the partial entry point currently visible, not a complete relationship graph. It can help locate places where scanner, request options, and `rev-list` parameters are adjacent; it cannot itself replace the caller's request or provide a JSON sample for the rename entry. Later, someone entered the file based only on the issue name and path and treated the file as the location of the complete implementation; this inference is no longer accepted.

## The old JSON approach is also retained

### Read the rename entry directly using old fields

In earlier years, when the original status JSON was unavailable, investigations searched for the rename entry directly using familiar old fields. This approach is now marked as no longer applicable. It did not distinguish between samples from the old entry and samples from the current entry, nor did it record the location of the actual JSON.

It is still retained because this explains why it was later required to store the original JSON separately. If the current case has only a secondhand account, do not polish that account into a field definition; if an original JSON is available, describe it by its actual fields and location, then decide whether it needs to be compared with the old sample.

### Write the two symptoms as a single anomaly
The early notes placed revision traversal and rename entry side by side, making them read like two phenomena in the same chain. This wording has been superseded by later branches. The revision parameter checks can continue to the scanner; the field checks for JSON must rely on the original JSON. When both occur in the same instance, they can appear in the same event record, but each must have its own supporting material and stopping point.

## Adjacent issues not yet split out

The meeting endnotes once included "add a caller example" and "reconfirm object ownership". These two statements were not accompanied by examples or new code snippets, so they were not expanded into a responsibility table.

They are not a single gap, either. The caller example is missing the local relationships in the request, `ScanRefsOptions` or `rev-list` arguments; the question of object ownership arises because the full implementation cannot be inferred from the file path alone. When new material becomes available, it should be added separately to the revision parameter branch or the side note on the file entry point, rather than merged into a vague statement that "the relationship needs verification".

rename entry also has unresolved issues of its own: the currently actionable steps are to preserve the original JSON, entry point information, field names and locations; without the original, stop at the missing-example stage. The page does not contain enough material to draw a conclusion about field compatibility across entry points, so the old examples can only be retained as historical references.

## Latest addition: checkpoints for commit-only requests

The following requirements were added after the old tree, the on-call addenda, the failure attribution and the changes of position during review. They address only commit-only revision traversal and do not replace the preceding status JSON branch.

For `CommitsOnly` requests, the checkpoint is at the conversion from `ScanRefsOptions` to `rev-list` arguments. The current behavior is as follows:

> A CommitsOnly ScanRefsOptions request omits --objects from rev-list arguments while still scanning the requested revisions.

This changes the interpretation of the old note that "no objects means an anomaly." When `--objects` is missing, first confirm that the request is indeed `CommitsOnly`, then confirm that requested revisions are still being scanned. If both can be confirmed, missing `--objects` does not by itself constitute an anomaly; if either cannot be confirmed, retain local fragments of the request and arguments, return to the revision entry point, and do not attribute it to the old object database.

```text
revision result looks like it contains only commit
├─ cannot confirm request type
│  └─ save request and arguments; do not use the old missing-objects determination
├─ request is not CommitsOnly
│  ├─ arguments contain --objects
│  │  └─ continue checking against the original parameter/result relationship
│  └─ arguments do not contain --objects
│     └─ stop at the request-to-parameter conversion, record the discrepancy
└─ request is CommitsOnly
   ├─ requested revisions are still being scanned
   │  └─ do not treat missing --objects as an anomaly
   └─ requested revisions were not scanned
      └─ retain the request, arguments, and entry location, and review the revision input path
```

The stop condition for this branch is much narrower than the old "check the object database first." It only describes the parameter shape under `CommitsOnly` and the relationship between requested revisions and scanning; it does not cover all combinations of scan options, nor does it invent a root cause for a situation where arguments already match but the result is still anomalous.

## status JSON remains in its own branch

Recent revision requirements did not add field definitions to the rename entry. The check for status JSON remains independent: preserve the original JSON, write out the rename entry's actual fields, the entry position, and adjacent objects; keep the old-entry sample and current-entry sample separate. If the original JSON is unavailable, only record that the sample is missing.

When there is a JSON original artifact but not enough current entry material for comparison, you may record the entry discrepancy, but must not turn old field names into current commitments. Conversely, even if the arguments requested by `CommitsOnly` have been fully explained, that does not establish that the rename entry for status JSON is sound. The two evidence branches must each be independently closed against their own original artifacts.

## Retained historical examples

**Historical example A:** The record showed only commit, so the note said "objects were not passed; check packed fallback". This explains why it initially switched to the object-reading path; later review did not accept this direct attribution. It can now serve only as a historical misreading and cannot be used to skip comparing the request type and arguments.

**Historical example B:** A rename entry appeared for status JSON, but no JSON original artifact was left behind, and the data was subsequently read using the old field name. This example cannot prove that the current field still exists. When revisiting a similar case, first obtain the original JSON, then record the actual field and location.

**Historical example C:** Based only on the issue name and call name, the investigation entered `lfs/gitscanner_refs.go`, and then treated the path as a complete relationship graph. The path remains valid local navigation, but cannot replace the request fragment, arguments, or the JSON original artifact.

## Points where you can stop while on call

- revision did not enter scanner: retain the request and entry observations, and return to the reference prefix or caller parameters.
- Already entered scanner, but `ScanRefsOptions` or `rev-list` arguments cannot be obtained: record only the gap.
- The request is `CommitsOnly`, and requested revisions are still being scanned: do not separately flag the absence of `--objects` as an anomaly.
- JSON has no original artifact: record only the missing sample; do not guess the fields in the rename entry.
- The JSON original artifact came from the old entry: retain the entry discrepancy; do not write the old field directly as current behavior.

This page still retains the initial quick judgments about objects and old fields because they are part of the history of this troubleshooting record. New cases should use the later commit-only branch and the JSON original-artifact branch; for anything that cannot be confirmed from the case materials, stop at the corresponding entry.

# Decision on ref Parsing and Commit Collection

This page preserves a side-by-side history of the work, not an interface specification that fully documents ref behavior. The early title put `ref parsing and prefix compatibility` and `eager commit collection` together, making them read like two successive steps in the same change. The material actually left behind was not so tidy: on one side were the type and function declarations in `git/git.go`, and on the other were requirements for covering user-visible entry points that appeared only later.

People still revisit the old page by the issue name. Its value lies in pointing people to the file, not in determining call relationships for them. This entry point remains here, along with the early habit of using "start looking here" too broadly; the qualifications added later serve only to explain why this record did not reach a more definitive conclusion.

## Scope Chosen for the First Draft

The first draft faced two options.

- Treat prefix compatibility as a local issue around ref types, ref names, and parsing functions, and first record the visible objects;
- Continue tracing the parsing functions to their uses, then bring the parsing results and commit collection into a single narrative.

The first option was chosen at the time. This decision was not a claim that the second was unrelated, but a refusal to substitute one file's declaration list for an examination of callers and user paths. `eager commit collection` was left on the page so that the other half of the title would not disappear; it was not treated as a completed result.

The terms retained for checking in the early text were local, remote, branches, tags, short name, and HEAD. They came from the breakdown of ref forms at the time and are useful as search clues. That version had no compatibility matrix, nor did it specify what each of these forms should return. Looking back now, the gap is obvious, but later expectations should not be retroactively written into the first draft.

## Objects Actually Visible Around the File

`git/git.go` is this page's only stable code entry point. The declarations that can be located are as follows:

|Object|Purpose on this page|
|---|---|
|`RefType`|Retains a starting point at the ref type level|
|`Ref`|Retains a point where names and types may intersect|
|`CommitSummary`|Indicates that the file also touches commit summary objects|
|`LsRemote`|Function entry point for remote input|
|`ResolveRef`|Parsing entry point for a single ref|
|`ResolveRefs`|Parsing entry point for multiple refs|
|`CurrentRef`|Entry point for the current ref|

The file header is `package git`, and there is an import block. Beyond that, the first draft did not copy any fields or interpret the type names as a complete data model. In particular, the presence of `CommitSummary` in the same file does not automatically mean its relationship with eager collection has been established; it merely reinforces the impression that "the two tracks may be connected through the same file."

The visible signature of `LsRemote` is:

```go
func LsRemote(remote, remoteRef string) (string, error) {
```

This is enough to let subsequent checking start from the remote parameter. It is not enough to show how the return value is used in later parsing, nor is it enough to show that local and remote follow the same branch. The early notes did not fill in this part, and leaving the gap intact is closer to the decision at the time than adding a passage of speculation.

## The Two Tracks Were Not Connected at the Time

The parsing compatibility track starts around `RefType`, `Ref`, `ResolveRef`, and `ResolveRefs`. The commit collection track asks questions further downstream: whether the user-visible entry point triggers collection, and whether existing tests or examples can cover that entry point. The two may meet during further investigation, but the available material provides no chain leading directly from the parsing functions to the collection results.

The first draft therefore adopted a conservative, though somewhat rough, division: record the former as a file-local area of observation, and mark the latter as pending review. This division continued to be used later and can easily lead readers to mistakenly think that the file is unrelated to the requirement; that is not accurate either. A better reading is that the file provides the first object to revisit, but does not yet provide the final behavior.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> DeclarationInventory
    DeclarationInventory --> ParsingCompatibilityTrack
    DeclarationInventory --> CommitCollectionTrack
    ParsingCompatibilityTrack --> PendingReview
    CommitCollectionTrack --> PendingReview
```

The two branches in the diagram indicate that the records were kept separately, not runtime state transitions. This also explains why the early decision did not try to arrange `CurrentRef`, remote input, and commit collection into a single sequence: no such sequence exists in the material on this page.

## Work Revisited Later

`HIST-206` is the navigation entry point for a regression in results after the ref parsing upgrade. The card later moved into an in-progress stage, showing that this track did not disappear when the first draft ended. The to-do on the card is specific: add repository tests based on the user-reported "ref parsing and prefix compatibility" examples, and preserve the current failure text or output bytes.

This to-do changed how the page is consulted. Previously, only the declarations and names in `git/git.go` were examined; later, at a minimum, the examples from user reports had to be brought back into the tests. It left behind no failure text, nor any result showing that a particular prefix had been fixed. This page therefore retains only the fact that "the regression was taken up again," without presenting it as a verified compatibility conclusion.

`HIST-222` is another entry point for eager commit collection. It requires using existing tests or examples to trigger the user-visible entry point and recording any user paths not yet covered back on the card. This requirement is more actionable than the early "look at user paths next," but it is still a verification action, not a record of a completed experiment.

The two cards appeared after the first draft, so the old version did not reference them. Their card numbers are added here now so that later readers can find the respective tracks of work, not to recast the cards' statuses, descriptions, or to-dos as evidence that the first draft already had.

## The Old Wording Retained

> For ref parsing issues, first look at `git/git.go`; prefix compatibility can be checked from the ref type and name entry points, and for eager commit collection, look at user paths next.

This passage still works as a locator, but should not be quoted on its own. The "first look" in the first sentence indicates only a starting point, not that the file owns the entire implementation. The "can be checked from" in the second sentence gives a direction for checking, not a claim that local, remote, branches, tags, short name, and HEAD have each yielded consistent results. The final sentence also merely leaves the collection issue to user paths, without stating which test or example has passed.

The old wording was not deleted because it accurately reflects the boundaries chosen at the time: not yet expanding a declaration file into a full compatibility commitment, and not yet mixing commit collection into the parsing issue. Its shortcomings also need to be retained: there was no account at the time of the order in which `ResolveRef` and `ResolveRefs` were used, no record of where the return value of `LsRemote` went, and no preserved observations of `CurrentRef` for specific name forms.

## The Decision This Page Ultimately Retains

The decision remains to record the two tracks separately. For ref parsing and prefix compatibility, begin the review in `git/git.go` with `RefType`, `Ref`, and the parsing functions, and continue checking with the name forms from the old record in mind. For eager commit collection, do not infer from the types or function names in the same file that the user entry point is already covered, but instead turn to the results of triggering it through tests or examples.

This decision comes at a cost: readers cannot obtain a complete compatibility conclusion from this page alone, nor can they know the state of eager collection across all paths. The benefit is that adjacent terms have not been pieced together into an implementation chain that has not been reviewed. For the record at the time, this was more appropriate than filling in all the blanks.

`DOC-17` is adjacent interface review material on checkout path restoration and blob byte and size units. It can serve as another review entry point, but it does not supply the ref parsing relationships left undocumented on this page.

Two actions remain unfinished: add repository tests based on the examples reported by users, and save the failure text or output bytes; use existing tests or examples to trigger the user entry point for eager commit collection, then write the uncovered paths back to `HIST-222`. Even after these additions, this page remains a historical record of the earlier work, intended for locating information and cross-checking, and should not be treated as the sole basis for the current compatibility rules.

# Object Database Root Identity Decision Record

Earlier investigation notes traced the issue name and call name to `git/odb/object_db.go`. This path is a useful starting point for verification, but it cannot establish object database root identity on its own. ## Two approaches considered at the time

One approach recorded root directly as a filesystem directory. This made lookups straightforward and was easy to connect to shard paths and filesystem object sharding, but it reduced object-layer identity to a location on disk. With the two storage forms filesystem-backed and in-memory, the same object database concept could leave different directory traces. This approach could not reliably explain why they belong within the same interface boundary.

The other approach treated root first as an identity at the object database layer, with the specific storage mechanism as an implementation attribute. This preserved the object relationships seen by callers and allowed further investigation of filesystem paths, packed fallback, or an in-memory implementation as needed. The trade-off was that the filename alone could not establish which implementation it belonged to; reference locations for the corresponding revision had to be retained.

This decision adopts the second approach. In the requirements history, root denotes the root identity of the object database; directories, shards, and storage media serve only as implementation-side clues. `git/odb/object_db.go` records local declarations and nearby navigation pointers; it is not automatically taken to identify a unique implementation. The earlier judgment that "seeing this file is enough to close this out" remains in the historical record, but is no longer the decision in effect.

The public interface side confirms root's public semantics and illustrates them with interface examples and caller-visible results; the core implementation side uses references from the same revision to confirm which kind of object database it actually connects to. If they use the same representation, prioritize adding tests at the existing filtering layer rather than introducing a new set of history path rules.

versions.body:
# history Path Filtering Proposal

This draft began with a narrowly focused question: history path filtering looks like a filtering problem, but neither where the path in history traversal comes from nor when it becomes a filtering condition has been clearly documented. `filepathfilter/filepathfilter.go` was initially noted because earlier investigation leads pointed to it. What is visible in the file is the `filepathfilter` package and its direct import relationships; this is enough to serve as a starting point for reading, but not enough to declare that the filtering logic belongs to any single layer.

The approach from the initial draft is retained here: do not start by adding a neatly named set of semantics to the interface, and do not infer what a non-match looks like from the word "filtering". First record one successful call and one failed call, then look at the path passed in at the time, the objects traversed, and the final visible result together. Here, a "failed call" only means that the expected visible result was not obtained; it could be a non-match, or the way the call was made, the path representation, or the traversal scope could be wrong. Without sample inputs, these meanings must not be conflated.

The two questions listed at the time have not gone away just because another review was added later.

- Does the path come directly from a history object, get assembled during traversal, or get normalized by the caller before entering the filtering layer?
- Do the terms include, filter, matching, and subpaths all refer to the same kind of comparison target at the call site?

Unless the first question is tied to a concrete call, subsequent claims of "subpath support" or "history filtering support" are only wording, not an implementable contract. The second question is particularly easy to misread: whether the same path has a prefix at different stages, and whether directory boundaries are retained, can cause seemingly identical conditions to produce different results. No answers are prescribed here; the only requirement is that the trial materials show where the answers come from.

## Scope After This Round of Review

HIST-212 placed the issue under "investigation of the scope of affected modules" and required visible results to be recorded separately for a successful call and a failed call. The card later confirmed ownership of the follow-up investigation, but the public follow-up note still identified missing concrete inputs, so implementation is not proceeding. This is a reasonable stopping point: without reproducible inputs, directly changing the filtering layer would only turn assumptions into fixed behavior.

The goal of this proposal is therefore not to define the final matching rules for history path filtering now, but to use the fewest samples needed to determine whether the following three things can be discussed separately:

1. Which layer owns the raw path;
2. Which layer treats it as a filtering condition;
3. Which layer presents the filtered results to the caller.

These three things may ultimately be handled by adjacent pieces of code, or two of them may be handled in the same place. The proposal does not assume an answer. During review, first trace the package and import relationships around `filepathfilter/filepathfilter.go` to find the actual entry point, then work back from that entry point to see where the path appears. Once the call site is found, record the value actually passed in at that site, rather than inferring what it "should" represent from the variable name.

## Why Not Make Changes Directly

The first approach considered was to add a stricter comparison in the current filtering layer to exclude history entries that clearly do not meet the conditions. The problem is not the size of the change, but that the failed sample has not yet shown where the failure occurs. If the path has already been processed before entering that layer, tightening the comparison in the filtering layer would only change the symptoms; if the paths themselves come from different sources, any single-point fix could make one call look normal while leaving the other still without results.

The second approach was to first standardize the path used in history traversal into a single form, then have all filtering entry points use it. This direction is not being adopted for now. A uniform representation sounds clean, but there is currently no evidence that multiple representations actually exist across the existing entry points, nor any concrete input demonstrating that one representation should become the baseline. Standardizing too early would turn a scope investigation into a compatibility rework, with the changes instead obscuring the information needed for the trial.

The third approach is to add only call samples and result records, then use those records to decide where to focus next. This is the approach currently adopted for the trial. It makes no commitment to interface changes and makes no claim that the existing implementation is wrong; its value is that the next discussion can refer to the same pair of inputs and visible results, rather than each person using the phrase "path filtering" to explain different phenomena.

This does not mean that every observation must become a formal test. The first round of materials only needs to be sufficient to answer one limited question: whether the two calls enter the same filtering entry point, and whether the path before and after that entry point can still be compared side by side. If not, first document where they diverge; if so, only then is there reason to continue examining the comparison behavior itself.

## What the Samples Must Capture

Record each call as one complete end-to-end chain, rather than splitting it into a separate "input table" and "results table". This avoids later pairing a result with the wrong path. Each record must include at least:

- Which identified entry point the call uses, or that the entry point has not yet been located;
- The exact path passed in;
- The scope of objects covered by that history traversal;
- What the caller actually saw after filtering;
- Why this result was labeled a success or failure.

The last item must be written as an assessment of that specific run, not as a predefined category. For example, success may simply mean that the caller received the items it needed to see at the time; failure may simply mean that the caller did not get the expected result. Do not arbitrarily reduce a failure record to "empty results", or expand a success record into "proof that all path values can match". The two samples serve only to locate the divergence, not to prove coverage of every path form.

If the raw path cannot be captured for one of the calls, the call can still be recorded, but the missing part must be made explicit: was the caller unable to provide the input, or did the traversal process not expose intermediate values. The former requires returning to the caller for additional material; only the latter may warrant discussing additional temporary observation locally. These two kinds of gaps require different handling and must not both be labeled "not enough logging".

When the samples produce different results, first categorize them using the following questions, in order, rather than immediately changing the logic:

- Whether both came from the same call entry point;
- Whether the path values before entering the filtering layer can be compared directly;
- Whether the scope of objects traversed is the same;
- Whether the difference appears only after filtering.

This is not a troubleshooting flowchart, nor an exhaustive list of possibilities. It only prevents a common misjudgment: seeing different results and attributing the difference to filter. Until the first two items are confirmed, the filtering layer remains only a candidate location.

## Scope Boundaries

This page only covers the trial materials for history path filtering and starting points for subsequent assessments. The callback path contract in tree traversal callbacks is an adjacent issue and remains in DOC-23 for separate handling. The fact that path appears in both places does not mean their conclusions can be shared: this page concerns the results visible to the caller before and after history filtering; the other concerns the conventions for paths supplied by callbacks. Directly transferring a judgment from one side to the other would skip the calling conditions specific to each.

Likewise, this page does not treat `filepathfilter/filepathfilter.go` as a catalog of repository-wide path rules. It provides a local starting point that can be revisited. If an actual call leads to processing outside the package, follow-up records should follow those call relationships, rather than forcing observations back here just to retain the original filename. Conversely, if both samples ultimately reach the same entry point, that alone does not justify assuming that they should share the same matching semantics; it is still necessary to check whether their path values are the same when they enter.

## When to Stop, When to Withdraw

Do not submit implementation changes before the concrete inputs have been supplied. The stopping condition for the current trial is not "a possible fix has been found", but that the two calls can be reviewed side by side, with no gaps in the raw path, entry point, or visible result for either call. Only after that condition is met should the next step be chosen: if the paths have already diverged before the entry point, return to the point of divergence for further investigation; if the paths are the same but the results differ, then consider the filtering comparison as a candidate location for changes.

If additional observation changes the results of the two calls but cannot explain what changed in the inputs or scope, withdraw the claim that treats that observation as a conclusion. It only shows that a variable has been added to the situation, not that the issue in history path filtering has been pinpointed. If the trial requires changes to public interfaces, a uniform representation for history objects, or callers to rewrite their own path, the current proposal should also be withdrawn and a separate proposal opened; those costs are beyond this scope investigation.

What is still missing is not more abstract rules, but concrete inputs. These need to be supplied in HIST-212 first. Once they are supplied, updates to this page should add only samples, entry points, and assessments supported by the samples; do not present implementation choices that have not yet been made as settled decisions.
