# Tree Callback Path Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the observed state; do not assign a cause yet.

The exception name has consistently been tree callback path. The old record used the problem name and call name to point to `lfs/gitscanner.go`, so this file is still the first one opened when investigating this type of issue. This entry point is useful, but "being pointed to by the file" and "the file carrying the complete call relationship" are not the same thing. The only partial information currently visible at the file header is:

```text
package lfs
import (
```

The terms path, tree, callback, repository, before, and commit all direct searches to the same place; they cannot, by themselves, prove where path is generated, nor can they prove that the exception occurred in the callback itself. This part of the old assessment is retained because it explains why people keep returning to this page to investigate; the conclusion is downgraded to an entry-point clue.

## Earliest Observed-State Fragment

The initial description was brief, stating only that a specific usage of tree callback path was abnormal. It contained neither the complete contents of the input tree, a sample path received by the callback, nor a comparison of the post-completion state. The early working hypothesis was that the repository state before the call or the commit boundary might affect how the callback handles path. This assessment was not supported by any counterexample at the time, so it cannot be treated as an attribution.

The troubleshooting wording at the time was "reproduce starting from the pre-call state." This wording remains valid, but two comparisons must be added: one tree entry from before the call, and one visible state after the callback completes. Posting only the exception name makes it impossible to tell whether the exception occurred at the entry point, in the middle of traversal, or during the post-completion state check.

The old paragraph also contains an implication that can easily be read as an established fact: since the record points to `lfs/gitscanner.go`, the exception should be resolved here. When tracing the path later, preserve this sentence's historical context; do not reuse it as an attribution judgment. What can currently be confirmed is the file entry point and navigation to its direct dependencies; the actual relationship must still be determined from references in the corresponding revision.

## Investigation Entry Point

When the same symptoms occur, first pin down the state before the call. At minimum, record the following adjacent artifacts, without changing their order:

- the current state of the repository;
- the commit being inspected and the tree corresponding to it;
- the path prepared to be passed to the callback before entering it;
- whether the tree entry can still be found at the original path after the callback returns;
- whether any additional visible changes appear after completion.

Here, "pinning down" does not mean creating another snapshot format. Save the existing output as is, especially do not save only the final line of the result. If the pre-call state was not recorded, even a successful reproduction makes it difficult to determine whether the change in path came from this processing or from repository state that already existed beforehand.

During troubleshooting, first record the raw value, then record the interpretation. The raw value includes the verbatim path, the verbatim tree entry, and the commit identifier; the interpretation should contain only "same", "different", or "not obtained". When the verbatim text has not been obtained, do not substitute "normal" or "restored". This page previously left several statements that could not be traced back precisely because it made local judgments more complete than the evidence at hand.

## Branch tree

```text
tree callback path anomaly
├─ A. Pre-call state not saved
│  ├─ Can we return to the same repository state?
│  │  ├─ No: stop at the entry point and add the state record
│  │  └─ Yes: collect tree, path, and commit again
│  └─ Cannot confirm that it is the same state: do not compare results; retain unknown
├─ B. Pre-call state saved
│  ├─ Is the path received by callback different from the entry-point path?
│  │  ├─ Yes: trace back along path to where it was generated, then inspect the corresponding tree entry
│  │  └─ No: enter the state branch after callback completion
│  └─ Cannot find the tree entry using the recorded path?
│     ├─ Yes: check the commit/tree cross-reference; do not modify callback first
│     └─ No: continue observing the repository after completion
└─ C. callback completed
   ├─ Any additional visible changes?
   │  ├─ Yes: retain before/after, pause recovery actions
   │  └─ No: record no change, but do not close out the path anomaly
   └─ No completion state: return to the observation entry point, add the result
```

The "stop" in this tree has two meanings. The first is that the input state is insufficient; continuing would only mix different conditions together. The second is that a difference has already been observed, but it has not yet been matched to path, tree, and commit. The second case also must not be treated as recovery merely because there are code changes. First retain the original difference, and decide whether to rerun only after the object relationships can be matched.

## A: No pre-call state available for comparison

If there is only an anomaly description, first check whether the repository state from before the call is still available. When the state has already changed, do not treat the current tree as the original input; if the original state cannot be found, record "unable to reconstruct pre-call state", and stop the investigation here. This stop condition is intended to preserve the evidence at hand, not to make a negative judgment about the issue.

If you can still return to the original state, retrieve the tree entry and the path prepared to be passed to callback again. Put both in the same record. Adding only path and not tree still will not let you determine later whether path points to the expected object; adding only tree and not commit makes it impossible to tell which historical boundary was used.

If repeated calls in the same state produce different path values, first keep the original text from both calls side by side. Do not immediately describe this as randomness, caching or callback reentrancy. The current material does not establish these causes, nor does it provide output that can distinguish between them. The next step is simply to confirm whether the state before the two calls was truly identical, and whether both calls targeted the same commit.

If the same state produces the same path, but the visible changes after completion differ, preserve those differences for now as well. This behavior may shift attention from the path to the completion action, but there is not yet enough material to establish which layer changed the repository. Pause recovery actions here, to avoid overwriting the first run's before/after with the second run.

## B: The path changes between entry and the callback

When the path changes, record the values at three points: the value before entering the callback, the value the callback actually receives, the value used to reread the tree entry after completion. If all three are the same, this only shows that no rewriting was observed in this sample; only if they differ can you go on to ask at which boundary the change occurred. Without the third value, do not present a change in the callback's input parameter as the final result.

When the path changes but the tree entry can still be found, keep both path values for now, and do not summarize this as "normalization". The difference between the original path and the returned path may be merely representational, or they may correspond to different tree entry objects; without an item-by-item comparison, these two cases must not be conflated.

When the path changes and the tree entry cannot be found, return to commit/tree for comparison. First confirm that the tree objects being compared belong to the same commit, then check whether the path is being used for another historical object. The order matters here: if the commits differ, discussing the path first will incorrectly record a difference caused by a history boundary as callback behavior.

If the path has not changed, but the original tree entry cannot be found after the callback, you still cannot conclude from this that the callback did not use the path. In this case, save the tree read results from before and after completion, and confirm whether the reads target the same repository. The old records lack both items, so this branch has remained unresolved for a long time.

## C: The path is unchanged, but changes appear after completion

This is the branch most easily overlooked in the old investigation. Identical original path text, however, does not mean that processing has no side effects. Place the repository, tree entry and commit from before the call alongside the same-named objects after completion, first mark additions, disappearances or content changes, then decide whether to continue tracing back through the callback.

If changes appear only in the working tree after completion, record its relationship to the tree entry, but do not directly attribute the working tree changes to the callback. First confirm whether the working tree already had differences before completion. If this was not recorded, write "Cannot distinguish pre-existing changes from changes made during this run", rather than "The callback modified the working tree".

If the change appears in the results of reading repository history, continue by checking the commit boundary. At this point save the commit used before the read and the commit used after it; the final list or final path alone cannot tell you which layer of history was replaced. The old page grouped all such differences under path, while the current page retains this only as a branch pending verification.

If there are no additional visible changes, record the raw results showing no change and retain the initial anomaly description. Not observing a change on one attempt does not erase the anomaly, nor does it prove that all tree callback path usages are the same. In particular when the pre-call state, commit or tree has not been fully preserved, this result applies only to this sample.

## D: commit and tree do not match

First confirm the commit, then confirm the tree it points to. Do not reverse the troubleshooting order. When the tree entry appears identical, if the commit differs, keep the samples separate; the same path may correspond to different objects at different history boundaries, and the current page does not have enough records to combine them.

If the commit is the same but the tree differs, retain the original text of both tree copies and mark where each was obtained. Do not overwrite the pre-call tree with the current repository state. If only one copy can be obtained, stop at "missing the other copy for comparison", and do not infer from a single copy that the callback path contract has been satisfied.

If both commit and tree are the same, but the path results differ, return to branch B. At this point you can temporarily remove the history boundary from the hypotheses, but you cannot identify a specific line inside the callback as the cause; this page currently has no material that pinpoints that line.

If even the commit cannot be confirmed, remove any claims of "the same history" or "the same input". Retain only the object names actually obtained and the missing items. In the old records "start from before" can easily be understood to mean that before is already available; subsequent reviews should instead read it as an operational requirement, not as evidence that already exists.

## E: Interference caused by repository state

If the same path produces different results in different repository states, first group the results by state. Group only by state fields that have already been recorded, and do not introduce environment labels that were not present when the issue occurred. The current input provides no specific environment, commands or failure output, so do not invent command lines or version numbers here.

If one group reproduces the issue and another does not, save the before, commit, tree and callback path for each group separately. Do not treat the group that does not reproduce the issue as evidence of a successful fix. It may simply not meet the trigger conditions, and the actual difference still needs to be found by comparing the records for the two groups.

If none of the groups reproduce the issue, retain the initial anomaly description and the states already tried. Troubleshooting can stop here, but leave a record of the minimum material to collect next time: pre-call state, the original path text, tree comparison, commit comparison and changes after completion. Do not change "not reproduced" to "recovered".

If only the repository after completion is saved, the state before the call cannot be inferred retroactively. The recovery action should be to collect additional evidence, not to clean up or rewrite the repository first. Cleanup will delete state that the anomaly may depend on, and even if the callback is normal afterward, the original question still cannot be answered.

## F: callback completion boundary

Record the periods before and after the callback returns separately. Before it returns, inspect only the path, tree, and commit it received; after it returns, inspect the tree entry, repository, and working tree. Combining the two phases on one line will omit when the change occurred.

If the callback returns no result, record "completion status not obtained". Do not use a successful call, process termination, or the absence of an obvious error as a substitute for callback completion. The current record does not provide an exception type or output format, so retain only the status gap here.

If the callback returns a result but the path is not the expected value, first retain the returned value and the entry value. Do not add a new path mapping table to this page; no mapping relationship is currently frozen. When checking the mapping, return to the corresponding revision of `lfs/gitscanner.go` and verify it along the actual references.

If the tree entry is still visible after the callback returns, record its path and the commit it belongs to. If it is not visible, record its last visible location. Both cases require before/after; "visible" itself is not a determination of the contract, only a branching condition for the next lookup.

## Old recovery actions

Previous records treated "run it again" as the most natural recovery direction, but did not leave enough before/after to compare the two runs, nor side-by-side values for path, tree, and commit. Therefore, a rerun can only be a data-collection action, not a verified fix.

Another common action is to directly adjust the path passed in by the caller. If attempting this, first copy the original value, then save a tree comparison before and after the adjustment; without this set of materials, the change will mix the original anomaly with the new input. This page does not retain an unrecorded "correct path".

If someone suggests cleaning the working tree or rebuilding the repository first, first clarify whether the original state is still needed. If it is needed, do not clean first; even if it is not needed, preserve the state before cleanup. Cleanup changes the observed state, so the clean result cannot subsequently be treated as evidence that the original problem disappeared.

If someone suggests looking only at the commit list, return to branch D and add the missing tree entry and callback path. The commit list can help locate the historical boundary, but it cannot replace a path comparison. If only the list is obtained, the investigation stops at "object relationships incomplete".

None of these actions has produced a successful result in the existing materials. They can serve as candidate actions within a branch, but cannot be written as the endpoint of the recovery steps. The old plan is kept here because people who consult this page later will still try these directions; "candidate" and "validated" must be kept separate.

## Changes left by subsequent review

HIST-213 later saw `qa_reproduced`, followed by `work_started (To Do → In Progress)`. This shows that the symptom at least reached the reproduction and handling stages, but the record does not provide the reproduction input, a path comparison, the tree contents, or the differences after completion. Therefore, these two actions cannot be written up as reproduction results, much less used to declare that the contract is already stable.

The reproduction node can only move the investigation from "whether there is an actual case" to "needing to find the case data"; the handling node only shows that someone continued investigating from the entry point. If you open the card again, first look for the original text corresponding to the four objects on this page: the state before the call, callback path, tree entry, and commit. If any one is missing, stop as directed by the branches above.

This card is the navigation entry point for this page. Do not use it as a substitute for the code path, and do not treat the card's action names as an explanation of the anomaly's cause. Keep only this local relationship between the page and the card: the card records event actions, `lfs/gitscanner.go` provides the code entry point, and this page preserves the order of objects that need to be checked between the two.

## Minimum on-call record

When time is short during an incident, write down five lines first, and do not start with a conclusion:

```text
before repository state:
commit:
tree entry:
callback path:
after visible change:
```

Leave fields with no data explicitly blank. If you cannot confirm something, write "not obtained", and do not guess from context. If you can fill in only two of the lines, fill in the original path and commit first, and state that the other three items are missing; do not hide the blank fields behind a summary.

If the anomaly disappears after the first call, still save the five lines from the first call. A successful second call can only serve as a separate set of samples. If the anomaly grows after repeated calls, save before/after for each call, and do not keep only the last one. Repeated calls themselves may change the repository, so a later result cannot directly represent an earlier one.

If the path is empty, contains a special form, or cannot be saved verbatim, retain the empty value or original output, and do not replace it on your own with a path that looks reasonable. The representation of the path is itself part of the current problem. If the original output cannot be obtained, return to branch A.

If the tree entry cannot be read, record whether the read occurred before or after the callback. Different read positions require different next steps; if it cannot be read beforehand, you cannot determine whether the callback caused it to be missing, and if it cannot be read afterward, you still need to compare against the results from before completion. Without a marker indicating the read position, the record has limited value.

If a commit appears on only one side, it cannot be called the same commit. Retain the side you have obtained, and list the other side as an object still to be collected. This small difference once caused older records to conflate the path issue with the history boundary.

## Recheck order

The first step is still to obtain the original text from the existing incident data. For the second step, open `lfs/gitscanner.go`, and first inspect the file header and the local declarations adjacent to tree, callback, and path. For the third step, follow the actual references in the corresponding revision to confirm the call relationships. For the fourth step, compare the relationships seen in the code against the five lines of incident data, item by item.

Do not infer implementation ownership from file locations, or guess the lifecycle of path from function names. Code navigation only answers "where to look"; records from the actual run answer "what happened this time". If local declarations cannot explain a change, leave that change unconfirmed rather than filling in a call chain unsupported by the evidence.

When the run records show that commit/tree matches and path also matches, but there is still an anomaly, retain the anomaly rather than recasting it as an environment issue. The current materials do not list any environment differences, so do not add environment names, version numbers, or commands based on experience. You may add "environment comparison needed" as a field to be filled in, but not as a difference already found.

When the run records show that path does not match, but the complete values before and after callback are missing, fill in the values first rather than changing the code directly. Only after the location of the difference is clear can you know whether to review entry-point preparation, callback reception, or reads after completion. The order of changes cannot substitute for locating the problem.

When records from the actual run are entirely missing and only the exception names for HIST-213 remain, the only actions this page can offer are to create a record and preserve the stopping point. Do not fill the gaps with related blob, memory-store, or other object exceptions; those topics belong to neighboring records, not to the materials already confirmed on this page.

## Retained old examples

Old example one: Record only "path anomaly", then designate `lfs/gitscanner.go` as the location for the fix. This example remains in the historical records because it explains the early lookup route; it is now marked as an outdated entry-point assessment. The correct way to use it is to open the file first, then trace back through revision references, rather than treating the file path itself as a responsibility boundary.

Old example two: No obvious change was seen after the call completed, so the issue was recorded as "no impact". This judgment is also insufficient. The absence of changes only covers the saved objects; if before, tree, or commit is missing, it can only be recorded as an incomplete comparison. Do not delete the old example, so that later readers do not mistake an incomplete sample for a negative result.

Old example three: Change path first, scan again, and finally retain only the new result. This sequence loses the original input and the first completion state. It is not currently listed as a recommended recovery method; if this has already been done in the actual run, at least save the path values before and after the change and the two states separately. If these materials do not exist, do not fill in differences.

## Areas that remain unresolved

This page has no fixed path that can substitute for evidence from the actual run, nor any caller that can be confirmed solely from a file location. Concrete failure samples for the tree callback path contract, additional visible changes after completion, and differences between repository states all need to be filled in from actual reproduction materials.

Unconfirmed items remain as they are:

- whether the path received by the callback is the same path passed in at the entry point;
- at which boundary the mapping between path and tree entry changes;
- whether the commit boundary played a role in this difference;
- whether any additional visible changes remain after the callback completes;
- which set of inputs `qa_reproduced` in the reproduction record corresponds to.

These questions should not be closed out by adding explanatory paragraphs. Once you have the raw output, return to the corresponding branch, and replace the blank entries with specific values; if you cannot obtain it, leave them unknown. Troubleshooting materials from earlier points in time can still be used for navigation, but should not be treated as the current authoritative guide.

# Commit Message Boundary Decision Record

This record is still retained because the early classification did affect the starting point for later reviews. The initial draft placed `commit message boundary` in the Tree and commit codecs group, without saying that the two checks shared code, merely recording them in the same place at the time. This distinction was not made clear in the initial draft, yet later readers of this page could easily interpret it as an implementation relationship.

The old framing is not being deleted. It reflects how quality checks were consolidated at the time: existing checks needed a place where entries could continue to be added, while the commit message boundary lacked sufficiently specific clues about the relevant objects. Listing it separately would have left an entry with no starting point; recording them together at least meant the review did not start from a blank slate. The cost was that the misreading caused by adjacent names was never addressed.

## The Choice Preserved in the Initial Draft

The comparison at the time was between recording methods, not codec implementation approaches.

| Approach | Decision at the time | Reason for adoption or rejection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record together with Tree and commit codecs | Adopted | The check names were adjacent, and existing quality reviews could continue to be recorded in one place |
| List the commit message boundary separately | Rejected | No object, call, or encoding location indicated where to start investigating if it were listed separately |
| Record it directly under a particular file or component | Rejected | No reference relationship supported attributing the implementation to it |

The first option does not mean "commit messages are handled by the tree codec", nor does it mean "the commit codec already covers commit messages". It only means that the two items were not split into two records at the time. The actual decision left by the initial draft was: when material is insufficient, retain the combined name for now, and do not fill in an implementation owner or implementation path based on guesswork.

This is an old decision. It has practical value, as well as clear gaps. Revising it to read as though boundary analysis had already been completed at the time would obscure why the later correction arose. This version therefore continues to preserve the "recording together" layer, while separating it from the current unconfirmed item.

## Corrections Added After Review

The later design comparison for HIST-216 brought this matter back under review. The correction in the card explicitly states: in the Tree and commit codecs section, one point regarding `commit message boundary` remains unconfirmed. What changes here is not the recording location chosen in the initial draft, but how that location is interpreted.

The earlier reading made it easy to mistake the umbrella term for an already finalized scope definition. After the correction, it can no longer be read that way: Tree and commit codecs may continue to appear as the old check name, but it cannot replace an independent assessment of the commit message boundary. The fact that the implementation has already been completed on an existing branch and entered review likewise cannot automatically fill in this boundary description; implementation status and record classification are two separate matters.

During the review, the old assessment was not rewritten wholesale as "nothing was ever confirmed". That would lose the facts in the initial draft: recording the checks together was indeed chosen at the time, and proximity in naming was indeed not distinguished from proximity in implementation. This part of the old assessment is retained so that later material can clearly identify which layer is being corrected.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> old_record
    state "Old combined record\nTree and commit codecs" as old_record
    state "Commit message boundary\nUnconfirmed" as open_boundary
    state "Old investigation entry point\njsonContext.go" as lookup
    old_record --> open_boundary: Review correction
    open_boundary --> lookup: Revisit
```

The states in the diagram are not an execution flow, nor do they indicate that the file already handles commit messages. It only preserves the sequence of changes to this record: the old name was adopted first; after review, the commit message boundary was separately marked as unconfirmed; the old investigation path remains available as a lookup entry point.

## The Note Left for Revisiting the Investigation

The old investigation record points from the issue name and call name to the following path:

`vendor/github.com/xeipuuv/gojsonschema/jsonContext.go`

This path corresponds to `internal/history-core`'s `v_prev`. The only local details directly visible in the file header are the package name and one import:

```go
package gojsonschema

import "bytes"
```

These details are enough to show that the old record used this file as a navigation point. They are not enough to prove that `jsonContext.go` implements the commit message boundary, nor are they enough to link `package gojsonschema`, `bytes`, and commit object handling in History Ledger into a single conclusion about where the implementation belongs. The conclusions that a path exists, that an issue name once pointed to it, and that the path actually lies along the call path are at different levels.

The retained path therefore has a very narrow purpose: when revisiting the old record, first confirm whether the issue name and call name in `v_prev` really lead here. If the references do not lead here, the navigation itself should be corrected, rather than forcing in a relationship to preserve the old classification. Even if the references do lead here, file adjacency, symbol references, the call path, and the actual boundary must still be distinguished; an earlier item cannot substitute for a later one.

The initial draft did not have this note for revisiting the investigation, so it was not in a position to decide which file the implementation belonged to. This version adds the path back to show where the old investigation started, not to elevate the path into a new implementation conclusion.

## Decisions in This Revision

1. Tree and commit codecs is no longer considered the confirmed implementation scope for `commit message boundary`.
2. The combined record in the initial draft is retained as a historical fact about how quality checks were organized at the time.
3. The commit message boundary is listed separately as an unconfirmed item; its review can proceed alongside the codecs review, but conclusions cannot be drawn automatically from the latter.
4. `vendor/github.com/xeipuuv/gojsonschema/jsonContext.go` continues to serve as the old investigation entry point and is not labeled as indicating where the implementation resides or who is responsible for it.

Here, "listing separately" concerns only the record and the boundary of the assessment. It does not claim that commit messages are necessarily separate in the data model, object database, history traversal, tree entry, or elsewhere. The available material does not establish these relationships, so this reorganization cannot be used to fill them in as a system structure diagram.

Splitting the entries adds the cost of one more lookup: readers who previously looked only at the umbrella term now need to see both the old classification and the current uncertainties. But this cost is smaller than the cost of continuing to make the umbrella term carry two layers of meaning. The umbrella term is appropriate for preserving the old set of checks; the unconfirmed item is the right place for boundary material obtained later. The two are kept in the same place, but no longer stand in for each other.

## Two Revision Approaches Not Adopted

One approach was to replace the old passages entirely with "the commit message boundary has always been unconfirmed". This was not adopted. This would look cleaner on the surface, but would erase why the initial draft adopted a combined name and make the later correction appear to have nothing to correct. The value of the old page as a reference is precisely that it preserves a classification that was not precise enough but was actually used.

Another approach was to assign the issue directly to the location of `jsonContext.go` based on the file path. This was not adopted either. The old record provides navigation based on the issue name and call name, while the file header provides local clues about `package gojsonschema` and `bytes`; neither provides the implementation chain for the commit message boundary. Recording this step directly as an attribution would be even more misleading than the old combined framing.

Some might also be inclined to retain the umbrella term, with only a line beside it saying "Note that this is unconfirmed". This approach was not continued after the review. The note is easy to overlook, while the umbrella term itself would still lead readers to believe that the scope had been settled. Separating out the unconfirmed item at least requires later records to state explicitly whether new material changes the old name, the entry point for revisiting the investigation, or the actual boundary.

## Card Entry Point and Outstanding Questions

HIST-216 remains the card entry point here. The card requires checking `commit message boundary` following the maintainer's routine steps, leaving parts without evidence blank. The same approach is followed here: "results still differ" is not written up as proof that a particular codec has or has not handled the matter.

What remains useful for now is the historical value of the old classification and the value of the old path for retracing the investigation. The unresolved points include: which objects the commit message boundary passed through during that review; the specific relationship between the old issue name and call name in `v_prev`; and which passage in Tree and commit codecs had included this check. Once any one of these types of material is obtained, revise only the corresponding layer, and do not overwrite the entire old record with a blanket conclusion that it has been verified.

# Alternative plan for commands integration testing

## Starting point retained on the old page

This route began with a specific integration-testing question: the same commands-client-integration object had two status entries in the records, but the caller was tracing both through the same entry point. The early draft split the issue into two routes, `clean checkout` and `packed fallback`. The initial instinct favored the latter because the two appeared to have different failure exit points. At that point, the callers using `reference prefix` had not been confirmed, nor had a decision been made on whether rollback would restore only the old entry point or also roll back the intermediate artifacts.

That reasoning is retained here. It was a working hypothesis at the time, not a default design confirmed later. The proposal still concerns the integration-testing route for commands-client-integration; the candidate must not be described as an entry point that callers have already adopted just because its name is shorter.

## First trial setup

For the comparison, keep one sample set for the original entry point and one for the candidate route. Use the same user, input, and observation window for both sets, changing only the route condition; the original input, version, and first visible result must not be replaced with cleaned-up green results. The candidate route was later documented as `rev-list`, but this only means using it as a comparison condition, not that `rev-list` has become commands · Client Integration's public entry point.

One green result does not end the trial. A trial with no real users, only display-label changes, or no way to restore `object database` on exit does not count as successful. If diagnosis does not get faster or misidentifications do not decrease, end the trial and restore the original entry point. Stop at the current interface boundary; do not mark parts the caller has not seen as successful.

Objections at the time focused on rollback costs, not on whether the candidate route could run successfully. `packed fallback` could collapse previously separate exit points into the same section of an integration-testing record; after a failure, the investigation would still have to distinguish between problems with the input, the version, or the object boundary. If rollback can only return to the old entry point, this cost must be documented clearly before the trial. If even `object database` cannot be restored, the sample set should not be expanded further.

## Checks added later

The local records for HISTA-005 put "whether the two statuses refer to the same object" back ahead of the comparison. The order of checks matters here: first review the two statuses in the order they occurred, then confirm object identity; a screenshot of the current entry point cannot substitute for confirming object identity. HISTA-009 also required aligning commands-client-integration with the current entry point while continuing to leave missing windows blank. This did not provide a result that could fill in those gaps.

After the toolchain was locked down, HISTA-013 recorded a narrower check: look at both the current entry point and the original current revision. This check collects evidence side by side; a nonempty result from either is not a substitute for the other. If the current entry point has a record but the original current revision is missing, that does not establish that the route succeeded; if both are missing, leave the outcome unknown.

These additions also changed how the earlier `path filter` was viewed. It is no longer just an ancillary parameter for the candidate `rev-list`; it affects which part of the relationships between objects the caller actually sees. However, the available material has not established its behavior across all failure exit points, so v3 still keeps it as an experimental condition rather than recording it as a decision. `resource close`, `parent boundary`, `tree entry`, and `qualifier` were also local observations raised during integration testing; they cannot be combined into a completed compatibility assessment.

## Why retain a route that was not adopted

`packed fallback` was not switched directly to the default route. It is suitable for a controlled comparison to see whether callers can diagnose issues faster and less often mistake the two statuses for a single object; but the records so far have not shown that it can preserve the old entry point during rollback, nor that `path filter` would not hide the boundary. The candidate `rev-list` has not been cleared for release either.

Only two rollback conditions can be confirmed: if diagnosis is no faster or misidentifications are no fewer, return to the original entry point; if `object database` cannot be restored, stop this trial immediately. The old records did not settle whether other intermediate states also need to be restored, so no automated step may be added here to fill that gap. The trial must not be recorded as successful just because the display labels have been made consistent.

## Gaps remaining after review

- The callers currently using `reference prefix` are not fully listed on this page.
- The validation window for the opposite input still lacks results; a single green result cannot substitute for them.
- Whether the combination of `path filter` and `rev-list` is worth pursuing remains undecided.
- Whether rollback should restore only the old entry point or also other state from the integration test remains undecided.
- The maintainer and trial start date have not been confirmed, so there is no roadmap commitment.

# Quality Signal Dual-State Postmortem

This anomaly was recorded in the Quality Signal Dashboard's test regression records: viewing the same object through the current entry point returned two different states on successive views. Both views pointed to the same set of failing samples, but the entry point supplied a different current revision each time, so there was no way to determine their regression classification as existing failures, post-recovery samples, or unstable signals.

The initial assessment was that the reference prefix did not match the old record and history might have been rewritten. This assessment explained only the mismatch between the entry point and the original record; it did not explain why the commit message had also changed. The two observations were not separated at the time, and the subsequent investigation spent a while focused on repeatedly reading the entry point.

## Timeline

- On the first comparison, the reference prefix in the old record differed from the one at the current entry point. The failing samples were still there, but their associated state could not be reused directly under the existing regression tiers.
- A later review of the retained records showed that the recovery page could retrieve the previous state. At one point this was recorded as "history rewrite is recoverable," meaning only that the recovery page could return the old content, not that the cause of the rewrite had been confirmed.
- On rereading the current entry point, the current revision had already changed from the first read. The two results had no common time marker, so they could not establish which had overwritten the other.
- Stopped retrying. Repeated reads added no information that could establish attribution; instead, they would mix outputs from different windows into the same failing sample.

## Impact

The Quality Signal Dashboard retains failing samples for test and uses regression tiers to distinguish stable failures from unstable signals. After the dual state appeared, the existing samples could still be retained as records of observed failures, but were no longer suitable for determining attribution within a particular regression tier. The separate schedule and maintenance work were not canceled as a result; the exit criteria did not change either. Signals from this window were simply no longer used to establish state consistency.

The original record and the recovery page are both retained in `docs/adj-git/incidents/git-quality-signal-board-same-object-two-states.md`. They are retained not to choose which is "newer," but to avoid being left with only the state last displayed by the entry point after recovery.

## Unconfirmed

The reason for the commit message change is still unknown. No records were retained that could be aligned to establish whether collection and execution changed between the two read windows, either. Missing time point: ____

This postmortem stops at what could be confirmed at the time; if the windows can be filled in later, only entries for the corresponding points in time should be appended. The two entry-point results should not be rewritten as a single continuous state.

2. Keep the final output. Once `status JSON` appears, do not clean up the environment; do not replace the final output with a summary from another page. # clean-checkout Window Decision Record

This record starts from a narrow question. In the clean-checkout windows review, Northstar Source Systems needed to decide whether the existing object-db entry point should continue to handle this part of the processing, or whether to shift control of the processing scope to window adjustments. Both sides used the word "checkout", but the review did not treat the entry point, the window, and the results seen by callers as the same thing.

An early draft first recorded a pragmatic choice: retain the current object-db entry point. This was not because window adjustments had been proven wrong, nor because the existing entry point could account for every checkout scenario, but because the material available to look back on at the time only supported a smaller scope of change. The meeting materials also stated keep old refs visible. This sentence was placed alongside the decision to indicate that old refs within the reviewed scope could not be silently removed as part of the entry point discussion.

## Two Paths Visible in the Old Records

| Option | What Could Be Confirmed at the Time | What This Round's Materials Did Not Resolve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current object-db entry point | The entry point was already a traceable subject in the clean-checkout windows discussion; visibility of old refs could remain part of the same round of checks | Whether the entry point covered other checkout paths; the precise definition of the window itself; whether callers saw the same results |
| Adjust window handling | The scope of control could be separated from the entry point discussion and studied further as a distinct handling issue | How adjustments would affect callers; whether old refs would remain visible; who would bear the compatibility cost, and within what boundaries |

So the decision at the time was not a vote between two complete designs. Retaining the existing entry point allowed continued use of a known path, while window adjustments remained an option that had not been adopted. Calling the latter a failed proposal would go beyond the record; calling it an approved proposal would introduce behavior that had not yet been specified.

## The Actual Disagreement in the Review

Those in favor of retaining the entry point were concerned with the order of changes. If the entry point and window changed at the same time, the visibility of old refs, the window scope, and the results seen by callers would all change together, making it difficult afterward to tell which change caused a difference. Keeping the existing entry point for now would at least keep this round's comparisons focused on something already observed. This reasoning supports only "do not replace it yet", not "the window does not need a definition".

Those proposing window adjustments were concerned that the boundary had been placed in the wrong location. If the window was where the processing scope was constrained, focusing only on the object-db entry point would make an implementation path look like a caller contract; callers might also treat a single observation as fixed behavior. This concern was not judged to be an implementation failure. What the review lacked was material on the results after adjustment, so it did not approve the sequence of changing the window first and then having callers adapt.

The objections did not establish that old refs could never change, either. They addressed the compatibility cost of this particular change: the meeting materials had already stated keep old refs visible, but did not specify conditions for removal, alternative ways to display them, or the scope of affected callers. Treating "they can be cleaned up later" as a side effect of window adjustments would amount to quietly introducing an unreviewed compatibility change into the decision.

## Where to Start Looking and the Limits of the Record

That round included looking back through `git/git.go` and several call names. This file was a starting point for investigation, not a declaration of permanent ownership. It could help place the object-db entry point back into the discussion at the time, but could not, on its own, explain all window behavior, how old refs were presented, or callers' full expectations of checkout.

That is also why the implementation story was not written up as an interface guarantee. Observations in the repository are tied to the time they were made; the same location may be only an implementation detail under a different form of window handling. What callers actually rely on needs confirmation from separate material. The review included only the entry point, window choices, and requirements for old refs that had already been examined in the decision, and did not use a file location in place of the missing compatibility description.

One verbatim statement recorded at the time was:

> Treat repository observations as dated evidence and keep the caller-visible contract separate from the implementation story.

Its role in this decision was very specific: a single observation can explain why this round did not rush to replace the entry point, but cannot incidentally create a long-term caller contract. Conversely, the results one can rely on when calling Fang Ke cannot be inferred solely from the implementation location either. Keeping these separate does not add another process, but prevents the discussion of window adjustments from prematurely becoming a compatibility commitment.

## What the Follow-up Review Changed

The follow-up review did not change "retain the entry point" to "adjust the window", nor did it add any new window categories. It changed two interpretations that the early wording could easily invite.

The first interpretation treated the entry point and the window as a strict either-or choice: since the entry point was retained, the window seemingly did not need separate handling. The follow-up review removed this inference, so retaining the entry point meant only that replacement had not been approved in this round. The second interpretation was that the entry point's continued presence was enough to establish stable window behavior. The follow-up review did not accept this either, because the visibility requirement for old refs was tied only to the reviewed scope.

The follow-up review also narrowed the supporting rationale to "a smaller change given the existing observations". This was not a long-term endorsement of the object-db entry point, nor an extrapolation to other checkout paths. It explained why this decision left the entry point unchanged for now, not why windows should not be discussed again in the future.

The sentence in the old draft stating that "old refs remain visible as required" also needs to be read within its scope. It can describe the portion covered by the requirements in the meeting materials, but cannot be expanded into a guarantee for every ref prefix, every repository, or every checkout entry point. If window adjustments return to review, a separate explanation will still be needed of what the adjustments cause callers to see and whether the handling of old refs changes as a result.

## Remaining Gaps

This decision did not finalize the precise definition of the window, specify the subsequent lifecycle of old refs, or provide a caller migration plan. It also did not explain whether other entry points had the same semantics. These gaps were not rejected proposals; the materials for this round simply did not bring them to the decision stage.

Thus, when referring back to this record later, what can be taken from it is a limited choice: the existing object-db entry point remains in place, window adjustments are not being used as a replacement action for now, and keep old refs visible remains within the checked scope. No new window boundaries or complete compatibility description can be directly inferred from these three points.

### Relationship Diagram Left by the Review

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[clean-checkout windows review] --> B[Retain the existing object-db entry point]
    A --> C[Adjust the window]
    B --> D[keep old refs visible]
    C --> E[Not approved in this round]
```

The adjacent object-store maintenance switchover handoff record is at DOC-44. Both sets of materials touch on terminology around the object store, but DOC-44 cannot fill in the window boundaries left undecided here, nor can it confirm the caller contract for this decision. What remains is precisely the disagreement left intact by that review: the entry point can stay for now, the window still needs a separate explanation, and the requirements for old refs cannot be deleted as implementation details.

# Reading the compatibility rehearsal entry

When tracing this path, the entry point and the landing point are not at the same layer. Start at the public repository entry for compatibility, then follow only one direct caller until you reach the first actual consumer in the release rehearsal. This order is more reliable than searching backward through files from `release`: same-named locations can provide clues, but cannot replace a call edge.

```text
compatibility public entry
        │
        ▼
   one direct caller
        │
        ▼
first actual consumer of release rehearsal
        ▲
        │ for locating
   migration ledger
```

### On the entry side

compatibility is the starting point for tracing back. First treat the public entry as the object of investigation, rather than pulling in every file in the repository where compatibility appears. What needs to be confirmed here is which direct caller the entry actually hands control to. Keep the caller to a single hop; just because similar names can still be found later, don't continue chaining adjacent files into a complete path.

Record the first relationship found from the entry side separately. It answers "who directly receives compatibility," but does not yet answer how release rehearsal is consumed later. When the two are mixed together, it's easy to mistake a helper location near the entry for the actual rehearsal consumer; the arrows on this page therefore stop at the first actual consumer.

### The position of the migration ledger

Use the migration ledger alongside this route. It helps the person taking this on line up the compatibility entry, the direct caller, and the release rehearsal consumption point, but its role is locating, not the call relationship itself. If the ledger text can point to multiple neighboring files, retain the one hop already confirmed on the entry side first; don't connect all of those files into the route just because their names appear in the ledger.

The ledger is also useful for finding the landing point after a name has moved. In that case, first compare the object with its position in the route, then return to the public entry to confirm the actual relationship. The old name in the ledger alone cannot establish that a file is still the long-term home, nor that it is the first consumer. A same-named file without a call edge is only a signpost; leave it beside the trace.

### `script/release.go` stop

This time, following `release` led to `script/release.go`. The filename and the match inside the file explain why it appears on this route, but this still isn't a complete source tour, and it does not leave a symbol name for this page to expand on. Treat it as the landing point on the release rehearsal side, and go back to the public compatibility entry to verify the direct caller; don't infer the entry's ownership from the position of `script/release.go`.

If this file is encountered from the release side first, the correct way to use it is to record it as a candidate landing point, then return to the entry side to verify whether it comes after the confirmed one hop and whether the first actual consumer of the rehearsal really appears after it. If all that can be confirmed is the filename and the hit `release`, stop the record here. The file's neighboring position in the directory cannot fill in the caller, much less substitute for another owner's confirmation of ownership.

### Actual trace-back

1. Open compatibility's public entry and first record the one-hop handoff it makes directly; don't expand to a second caller.
2. Follow this hop to find the first actual consumer in the release rehearsal; stop once you find it, and don't bring later links in the consumption chain into this page.
3. Use the migration ledger to compare object names and route positions, distinguishing ledger signposts from confirmed call edges.
4. Use `script/release.go` to recheck the landing point on the release side; if the file location changes, start again from the public entry, not from an ownership guess based on the old path.
5. If they don't line up, leave a gap: is the entry relationship unverified, or did the ledger and file location fail to line up? Don't use same-named files to fill the gap.

Early records contained only the entry topic, `script/release.go`, and an unresolved mapping. A later review clarified the reading order and also separated "one direct caller" from "the first actual consumer"; it did not state the missing symbol name, additional callers, or permanent ownership as established facts. This page keeps this limited route and stops at the boundary where confirmation from another owner is needed.

See DOC-46 for the discrepancy in the support handoffs window. That record covers changes on the ground; this page keeps only the trace-back route from compatibility to the rehearsal entry.

# support handoff discrepancy postmortem

This record covers a localized discrepancy during a support handoffs window. The outcome expected under the handoff plan did not match what was actually visible during the window. The first thing confirmed was the mismatch itself; at that point, it could not yet be directly attributed to a specific cause, nor was it treated as a problem with the entire support process.

## Sequence recorded at the time

First, someone noticed during the handoff window that the outcome differed from the original plan. What was captured at discovery was the observed difference, not a complete explanation assembled after the fact. A temporary recovery followed so that work in this window could continue; the record distinguishes "recovered" from "knowing why the discrepancy occurred." The recovery action cleared the immediate handoff blocker, but did not prove that the same discrepancy would not recur in the next window.

In the later review, the focus shifted from "whether the results were back" to "where the discrepancy first appeared." The replay material did not provide a verified root cause, only a control point that needed to be added to the process: "record the first divergent byte". Here, byte means the first unit of content in the replay that differs from what was expected; the purpose of the control point is to preserve the first divergence, rather than just record an overall failure at the end. Only then can the observations before and after the temporary recovery be compared without conflating them. This requirement was added to the record later and should not be retroactively described as a step already performed at the initial discovery.

## Investigation path

At the time, `vendor/github.com/kr/pty/pty_unsupported.go` was checked by following the call name support. This path shows where the investigation started at the time; it does not establish that the discrepancy should always be attributed to that file, nor can it substitute for the handoff observations themselves. The relationship between the file location and the organizational coordination window was not fully verified at the time.

This page therefore keeps three things distinct: the initial finding was a mismatch between the visible outcome and the plan; a temporary recovery did take place; and where the discrepancy first branched off and why it did so remain unconfirmed in this record. The earlier assessment of the window remains here because it reflects how the situation was handled at the time, not because it has since become the agreed account. If this page is cited again, first look at the first difference in the observations recorded at the time, then at the recovery action; do not cite only the three-character phrase "recovered" as a substitute for assessing the cause.
